input.question: how did computers get so smart at playing chess ?
input.ground_truth: Chess is a unique game, in that each piece has only certain moves that can be performed at any time, and thus one can predict which moves will be done many turns in advance, and each move to counter them. There is really no "randomness" in chance. This allows a computer to be programmed to constantly monitor the positions of each piece on the board, and do exactly that, think 10+ turns ahead and figure out each counterplay to each possible movement of each piece on the board, your own and your opponents. & #x200B; It's very close to what a grandmaster in chess does, however, a computer is not subject to stress or other interferences.

Question: how did computers get so smart at playing chess ?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a toy robot that likes to play chess. At first, the robot doesn’t know how to play at all. But every time you play with it, you show it what to do—like, “Oh, you should move this piece here!” or “That’s not a good move.”

Then, the robot plays with lots and lots of other robots and people. It remembers what moves worked well and which ones didn’t. It tries over and over again, learning from every game. It gets really good at remembering patterns and tricks, kind of like how you learn to tie your shoes after practicing many times.

Also, some very smart people wrote special instructions (called programs) that help the robot think really fast and look ahead to see what might happen next in the game. So, after playing millions of games and learning from them, the robot becomes super good at chess!
